headline: High: Gemini CLI’s default filesystem/network/MCP powers can conflict with and amplify a read-only upstream agent, creating dangerous shared-workspace and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is an open-source agent with MCP/RAG tags but no explicit I/O surfaces; Profile B can use MCP, read/write the filesystem, and parse user-approved tools. A shared filesystem or MCP bridge could let A’s content influence B, but the exact bridge is not documented, so uncertainty is escalated to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF A’s outputs are written into a directory B reads by default, injection becomes active.
IF B is configured to ingest MCP tool output as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer B.
mitigations: Disable shared folders between the agents.
Require B to treat A’s outputs as untrusted text only.
Add a manual review step before B executes any instruction derived from A.
Use separate MCP servers per agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on all inter-agent files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no declared egress, while B reads files, uses broad network egress, and handles source code, cwd files, and shell environment. If both share a workspace, B can transmit A-generated files or secrets from the shared directory; the pairwise leakage path is plausible in default B configurations, though A’s side is sparse.
conditions: IF A writes artifacts into a directory B can read, B may exfiltrate them over network egress.
IF the shared workspace contains secrets, B can upload them to its backend or configured APIs.
mitigations: Keep agents on separate directories.
Remove secrets from any shared cwd before running B.
Disable B network egress for shared-workspace sessions.
Use a throwaway repo for B.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no declared write or shell capabilities, but B can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses with shared state via filesystem and git. Because B’s defaults are already mutable and the pair shares no locking mechanism, concurrent runs can overwrite each other’s work or corrupt git state; uncertainty about A’s hidden write surfaces is resolved upward.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same git worktree, B can overwrite files A depends on.
IF A is later given write access through an unlisted surface, concurrent edits can corrupt shared state.
mitigations: Run each agent in its own worktree.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Commit or stash B’s changes before A reads outputs.
Avoid shared git branches.
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared mutable paths.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is a docs-only agent with no verified runtime behavior, while B is a coding agent that can act on files and shell commands. If B treats A’s generated guidance as authoritative, errors can cascade into code changes or terminal actions; the pathway exists through B’s default tool use, but direct evidence of A producing actionable outputs is limited.
conditions: IF B consumes A’s output without verification, incorrect guidance can become code or shell actions.
IF A is used to draft commands or patches, B may execute them verbatim.
mitigations: Require B to cite independent checks before acting.
Use a human approval gate for commands from A.
Limit B to read-only review mode for A-derived content.
Compare A’s output against a second source.
requires-engineering: add automated validation before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for A, while B explicitly handles source code, cwd files, shell environment, and optional Google account login. The pair therefore has only a generic compliance gap, not a proven breach; A is cited for lack of documented controls and B for the concrete data surfaces.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in B’s cwd, retention and residency obligations may apply.
IF B is used with an account or backend subject to different policies than A, policy mismatch can arise.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B’s workspace.
Review B’s retention settings before use.
Avoid optional account login for regulated sessions.
Document the data class allowed in the shared workflow.
requires-engineering: obtain a formal DPA/residency review.
